goodsIndustries.name: Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing & Hunting
goodsIndustries.analysis:
Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting sector GDP fell 1.1% month-over-month in the March 2026 reference period while holding up 2.1% year-over-year — the split reading1 tracks two sub-sectors moving in opposite directions, with the Saskatchewan farm canola price at $672.81 per tonne, unchanged on the week but up 1.8% month-over-month and 6.2% year-over-year.2 China cut its combined anti-dumping and countervail tariff on Canadian canola seed to roughly 14.9% effective March 1, 2026, down from a combined level near 84%, restoring access for approximately $4B per year of seed exports after China's 2025 canola imports fell nearly 50% under the prior tariffs.3

Forestry contracted as 21 permanent or indefinite British Columbia and Canada mill closures since 2023 removed roughly 15,000 forest-sector jobs since 2022 — Domtar permanently closed its Crofton, BC NBSK pulp facility (about 350 employees), even as lumber futures settled at $633.00, up 2.2% on the week and 6.4% over the month.45 The potash and fertilizer proxy Nutrien traded at $88.73, down 6.2% on the week and 8.4% over the month, a softer input-cost signal for grain growers.2

The project database tracks 734 combined agriculture and forestry records carrying roughly $8.2B in pipeline value — about 269 of those records sit in forestry and hold $4.7B.6 If China's reduced canola tariff holds through 2026, the roughly $4B per year seed export channel would remain open for Saskatchewan, Alberta, and Manitoba growers.3

goodsIndustries.name: Mining, Quarrying & Oil/Gas Extraction
goodsIndustries.analysis:
Mining, quarrying and oil and gas extraction GDP contracted 2.1% month-over-month and 1.5% year-over-year in the March 2026 reference period — the contraction1 ran against sharply higher metal prices, with the nickel proxy at $43.01, up 18.6% over the month and 100.3% year-over-year, and the iron ore proxy at $15.42, up 85.4% year-over-year.2 Cameco traded at $151.07, up 7.1% on the week and 60.5% year-over-year, tracking Saskatchewan uranium expansion and the small modular reactor supply chain.2

The federal government announced 30 critical-minerals partnerships in March 2026 unlocking $12.1B in project capital, plus $3.6B in new programs including a $1.5B First and Last Mile Fund and a $2B Critical Minerals Sovereign Fund — the Major Projects Office prioritized 13 projects, five of which are critical-mineral mines: McIlvenna Bay (copper), Red Chris (copper), Crawford (nickel), Matawinie (graphite), and Sisson (tungsten), with combined economic activity exceeding $60B.3 New records this period include BHP Jansen Stage 2 potash, Saskatchewan, $6.9B (Approved), and Horne 5 polymetallic, Quebec, $2.4B.4

The project database holds 812 mining and oil and gas records totalling roughly $298.6B, with 32 first tracked since June 13 — the highest new-discovery count of any sector this window — capital commitments precede production, so the pipeline grew even as sector GDP fell.5 If nickel and uranium prices hold near current levels, the five Major Projects Office critical-mineral mines and Saskatchewan potash and uranium expansions would advance.3

goodsIndustries.name: Utilities (Electricity, Gas, Water)
goodsIndustries.analysis:
Utilities sector GDP was flat month-over-month (+0.0%) and down 1.6% year-over-year in the March 2026 reference period — the reading1 sits against the single largest tracked project pipeline of any NAICS bucket, 936 power and energy records totalling roughly $614.3B.2 The uranium proxy traded at $26.86, up 3.9% on the week and 8.7% year-over-year, underpinning small modular reactor economics, while the Canadian infrastructure equity basket eased 0.6% on the week to $57.45 but held up 35.0% year-over-year.3

Ontario Power Generation applied in March 2026 to the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission for a Licence to Operate the first Darlington small modular reactor — governments committed up to $3B to the first unit within a $20.9B four-reactor program, and the federal nuclear and electricity strategy advancing through 2026 carries Wesleyville (up to 10,000 MW) and Bruce Power (up to 4,800 MW).4 Rose Valley Wind in Saskatchewan ($164.4M) entered construction this period with Canada Infrastructure Bank and First Nations backing.2

Nuclear and small modular reactor capital is pre-construction and not yet reflected in current utilities GDP — British Columbia's 2025 call for power links to 138 affected projects in the policy tracker.5 If the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission licence and the federal electricity strategy proceed on schedule, the reactor programs would convert committed capital into multi-year construction activity.4

goodsIndustries.name: Construction
goodsIndustries.analysis:
Construction sector GDP fell 0.6% month-over-month and 1.5% year-over-year in the March 2026 reference period — housing starts fell 6% to 261,377 SAAR in May 2026 from 278,380 in April, and building permits totalled $12.5B in April, down 7.6% month-over-month from a January peak of $13.3B.1 Lumber futures settled at $633.00, up 2.2% on the week and 6.4% over the month, a residential framing input, while the steel proxy eased 3.4% on the week to $105.35 yet remains up 68.3% year-over-year.2

Construction led May employment gains at +27,000 (+1.7%) even as the sector's output and start rate declined — non-residential construction capital expenditure is projected at $274.0B for 2026 (+5.9%) against projected non-residential starts of -7.8% year-over-year.1 The federal Build Communities Strong Fund ($51B) links to 2,196 affected projects and Ontario's Budget 2026 ten-year capital plan ($210B) links to 412.3

The project database tracks 1,926 infrastructure, residential, and housing records totalling roughly $265.5B, up 14 since June 13 — new this period are the Fraser River (George Massey) Tunnel, BC, $4.15B (Approved), and a BC homebuilding fees reduction and condo conversion program, $3.2B (Proposed).4 If lumber and steel input costs hold near current levels and federal and provincial infrastructure funds disburse, the pipeline would continue absorbing labour despite the start-rate decline.3

goodsIndustries.name: Manufacturing
goodsIndustries.analysis:
Manufacturing sector GDP rose 0.4% month-over-month but fell 2.5% year-over-year in the March 2026 reference period, the steepest annual goods-sector contraction — the annual decline1 is concentrated in tariff-exposed metals, with the steel proxy at $105.35, down 3.4% on the week yet up 68.3% year-over-year, and the nickel proxy at $43.01, up 100.3% year-over-year as a battery-cell input.2 Downstream aluminum manufacturing is down 14% and aluminum output is down about 2% to September under U.S. tariff measures.3

Canada extended its steel and aluminum tariff measures for one year in June 2026, maintaining tariff-rate quotas for non-CUSMA imports with above-quota volumes subject to a 50% tariff — support includes a $5B Strategic Response Fund and $1B in BDC financing.4 The electric vehicle and battery buildout continues, with Northvolt Six near Montreal expected to begin operations in 2026 (30 GWh, expanding to 60), NextStar (Stellantis and LG) in Windsor at over $5B invested, and Honda Alliston at C$15B.5

The project database tracks 365 manufacturing records totalling roughly $85.4B, up 2 since June 13 — primary metal and food manufacturing sit alongside transportation equipment, where the battery buildout concentrates.5 If U.S. Section 232 tariffs and the extended Canadian measures persist, tariff-exposed metals manufacturing would stay pressured while battery commissioning could add capacity through 2026.4
